processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: General processing of Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels: forging ingot homogenized at 1100–1250 °C for 1–3 h, then hot-rolled to 2–5 mm thickness between 1100 and 850 °C; a large rolling reduction provides recrystallization driving force.
Solution-treatment plateau (1100–1200 °C) of the Fe–Mn–Al–C processing route (Fig. 3). The quenched microstructure of A-BDP steels is reported to be full austenite.
Solution treatment followed by water quenching (listed as 'Solution-water quenching' in Table 2, row for Fe-21Mn-10Al-1C-5Ni), producing a fully austenitic (quenched) matrix.

structures.overall_structure: Quenched (solution-treated + water-quenched) A-BDP (austenite-base duplex phase) Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel. The quenched microstructure of A-BDP steels is full austenite (γ).

precipitates.distribution: precipitated in austenite under quenching / quenching-ordering annealing conditions

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Compiled mechanical properties from Table 2 for the A-BDP-type composition Fe-21Mn-10Al-1C-5Ni [54] processed by 'Solution-water quenching'; UTS and TE represent ultimate tensile strength and total elongation.

analytical_models.equation_role: predict density of Fe–Mn–Al–C steel from Al, C and Mn mass fractions
analytical_models.model_note: ρ = 8.15 − 0.101ω(Al) − 0.41ω(C) − 0.0085ω(Mn); C content most strongly reduces density, but density is mainly controlled by Al and Mn.

analytical_models.equation_role: compute austenite lattice constant from Al, C and Mn mass fractions
analytical_models.model_note: a = 0.35721 + 0.0002771ω(Al) + 0.0044089ω(C) + 0.0001166ω(Mn); C expands the austenite lattice most strongly.

analytical_models.equation_role: relate yield-strength increment of austenite to individual Al, Mn and C contents (wt.%)
analytical_models.model_note: σ_yield = 10.5ω(Al) + 351.5 (Eq.3); σ_yield = 0.58ω(Mn) + 328.0 (Eq.4); σ_yield = 180.7ω(C) + 250.7 (Eq.5); C and Al raise yield strength more than Mn.

unmapped_findings: A-BDP steel composition window (Table 1): 10.0 < X_Mn < 25.0 wt%, 5.0 < X_Al < 12.0 wt%, 0.6 < X_C < 1.0 wt%.
A-BDP steel constituent phases listed in Table 1: α, B2, DO3, γ, κ, β-Mn (the austenite-base duplex phase assemblage of the alloy family).
After aging at 500–800 °C, lath-like ferrite forms along the austenite grain boundaries of A-BDP steels, with B2 phase found within the lath-like ferrite (b0045).

The deformation mechanism of A-BDP steels is strongly affected by the δ-ferrite fraction, the hardness difference between austenite and ferrite, and the ordered phases in ferrite (b0093); austenite generally determines the deformation mechanism when the δ-ferrite fraction is less than 10% (b0094).

In a Fe-27Mn-12Al-0.8C A-BDP steel (27% δ-ferrite fraction), nano κ-carbide also precipitated in austenite under quenching or quenching-ordering annealing conditions, and its size increased with rising ordering annealing temperature; coarse B2 and ultrafine DO3 particles precipitated in ferrite (b0101).

Room-temperature impact energy of A-BDP steels after solution treatment was much higher, even exceeding typical austenite stainless steel, with an obvious ductile-brittle transition below about −100 °C; after aging at 550 °C for 16 h the room-temperature impact energy dropped sharply (e.g. Fe-30Mn-10Al-1C close to 0 J), attributed to κ-carbide precipitation (b0121).
The impact toughness of Fe-Mn-Al-C austenite steels is higher under solution treatment + water quenching than under aging treatment (b0123).

A-BDP microstructure in the quenched state is full austenite; the room-temperature microstructure of single austenite Fe-Mn-Al-C steels is composed of equiaxed austenite together with annealing twins (b0044).
